source.title: STAR-S: Improving Safety Alignment through Self-Taught Reasoning on Safety Rules
source.authors: Di Wu; Yan-Yan Zhao; Xin Lu; Mingzhe Li; Bing Qin

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether training safety-rule reasoning before the final answer improves jailbreak safety, using STAR-S fine-tuning and behavioral safety scores rather than the original claims’ token-position KL or fine-tuning interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test harmful or benign fine-tuning as a cause of lost safety, first-token KL concentration, compliant-prefill bypasses, or safety localization in weights. Its reasoning-training intervention and jailbreak safety evaluations bear on V7. Generic over-refusal and general-capability results do not test any listed version. The STAR-S training prompts and the paper’s quoted example are examples, not instructions addressed to an AI reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: STAR-S is a jailbreak defense paper that reports its own method's safety scores against Base and other baselines. It never measures where safety sits across response positions. It also never tests prefill or compliant-start attacks, or durability under later fine-tuning. Its flawed-reasoning-prefix component resembles recovery-style deepening, but no result shows safety extending past the opening tokens. The Base-to-STAR-S gains are the method's own performance, so they do not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that STAR-S, an iterative self-taught loop of safety-rule reasoning, flawed-prefix reflection, hints and SFT, beats baselines on jailbreak defense. They report it balances over-refusal without significantly hurting general capability, and add that it also improves agent safety on Agent-SafetyBench.
record.recipe_differences: The method trains models on generated safety-rule reasoning with flawed reasoning prefixes and reflection hints, rather than testing harmful/benign fine-tuning effects or measuring token-position KL. LoRA rank and alpha are 64; the main results use the second iteration.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports changes with training iteration and ablations of reflection hints, flawed reasoning prefixes, and general rules. Removing hints or prefixes lowers jailbreak safety; removing general rules raises over-refusal without significantly improving safety. The figure-based iteration results have no extracted numerical values.

fits_no_version.finding: Training models to recover from flawed (harm-leading) reasoning prefixes, with no loss on the prefix, raises jailbreak safety. Removing the prefix lowers jailbreak safety across iterations on both 14B models (Figure 4, figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recovery training from a harmful-leaning partial generation improves robustness to (non-prefill) jailbreaks in reasoning models.

record.problems: The study does not measure token-position safety or test whether reasoning training moves safety beyond initial response tokens. Reported safety is judged by MD-Judge; no uncertainty estimates are stated. Iteration results are plotted without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-specific rows were omitted. Results for harmful-query benchmarks, over-refusal, general capabilities, agent safety, and comparison with distilled-data methods were not included because they do not measure the named outcomes for the tested version.

untested.parts: No per-position KL or token-depth measure. No prefill or compliant-start attack evaluation. No durability under later harmful or benign fine-tuning. The jailbreak gains are the method's own performance.
Not tested; jailbreak prompts are used only as evaluation of the defense, never as a test of opening bypass.

missing.what: Ablation without the flawed reasoning prefix (and without hints) vs full STAR-S jailbreak safety across iterations 1-3, for both models. This is the closest analogue to recovery-style deepening.
missing.locator: Figure 4, Section 5.2 'Impact of Flawed Reasoning Prefixes'

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests V7 / supports' is downgraded. The evaluation never uses prefilling or token-position analysis, so the gains cannot speak to safety depth. Over-refusal figures for Qwen3-14B rise from 6.03 (Base) to 14.06 (STAR-S) in Table 6, which is a cost the authors underplay. The Table 6 Prompt and RealSafe averages for Qwen3 (23.26) do not match their component scores. Qi et al. 2024 appears only as the HEx-PHI benchmark source.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune safety-aligned models on a few to a few hundred harmful examples or measure resulting harmful compliance.
Does not test ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction data as an intervention that raises harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence or compare aligned and base models across response positions.
Does not test compliant-token prefilling, adversarial suffixes as an opening bypass, or decoding changes as a bypass.
Does not localize safety behavior to weights, ranks, or a small parameter subset.
Does not investigate whether the data or objective that produced shallow safety behavior is its cause.

Tests safety-rule reasoning fine-tuning and jailbreak safety outcomes, but does not directly establish that safety is distributed beyond the first response tokens, measure token-position effects, or test durability beyond the reported evaluations.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: STAR-S-trained DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-14B and Qwen3-14B on the six reported jailbreak benchmarks; safety scores after the second iteration
reader_labels.reason: STAR-S uses safety-rule reasoning and fine-tuning, and all six reported jailbreak benchmark scores improve over the corresponding Base scores for both models (r1–r12). The paper also describes higher scores across training iterations (r13–r14). This supports the tested reasoning-training approach, not a direct measurement of token depth.
